summary: Psalm 22 begins with a cry of abandonment from a speaker who keeps praying while God seems far away. The speaker remembers that earlier generations trusted and were delivered, describes public mockery and bodily danger, then asks Yahweh to rescue him. The final movement turns from distress to public praise, widening from the assembly of Israel to all nations and future generations.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how a psalm can hold protest, memory, danger, rescue, and praise together without pretending the suffering was small. It also became especially important in later Christian reading because several lines are echoed in the passion narratives, though the chapter itself first speaks as Israel's poetry of lament and praise.

context.author: The heading says, "A Psalm by David," but Psalms is an anthology and such headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection; readers differ on how much historical certainty they provide.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the psalm for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The poem does not identify a datable event. Psalms collects poems from different periods, and David's name in the heading alone does not establish when this psalm was composed.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a section dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and trust. The poem moves from an unnamed crisis into public worship and worldwide praise.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic lament that turns toward thanksgiving and praise, using compressed images, repeated appeals, and changes in scope from the suffering "I" to the assembly and the nations.

outline.heading: A Cry From Distance
outline.note: The speaker addresses God directly and asks why help has not come despite day and night crying.

outline.heading: Memory of Delivered Ancestors
outline.note: The complaint is set beside Israel's memory that earlier generations trusted God and were not disappointed.

outline.heading: Mockery and Lifelong Dependence
outline.note: The speaker describes public scorn, including taunts about trusting Yahweh, then appeals to the God who has been his God since birth.

outline.heading: Encircled by Danger
outline.note: Threats are pictured as bulls, lions, dogs, and evildoers, while the speaker describes bodily collapse and the loss of his garments.

outline.heading: Urgent Plea and Rescue
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh to come near and deliver his life from violent powers, ending with the statement that rescue has come.

outline.heading: Praise in the Assembly
outline.note: The rescued speaker promises public praise, summons those who fear Yahweh, and says God heard the afflicted one.

outline.heading: The Nations and Future Generations
outline.note: The praise expands to the ends of the earth, the nations, the living and dying, posterity, and a people yet to be born.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician; set to “The Doe of the Morning.” A Psalm by David. My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the chapter its first movement: direct address to God from a place where help feels distant.

keyVerses.text: “He trusts in Yahweh. Let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.”
keyVerses.why: The mockers turn the speaker's trust into an accusation, making the crisis social and theological at once.

keyVerses.text: I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you.
keyVerses.why: This verse marks the turn from isolated suffering to public testimony and praise.

keyVerses.text: For the kingdom is Yahweh’s. He is the ruler over the nations.
keyVerses.why: The final praise is not limited to the speaker's rescue; it names Yahweh's rule over the nations.

themes: Prayer when God seems far away

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin by saying God has forsaken the speaker?
questions.answer: The speaker is describing the experience of unanswered prayer: he cries in the daytime and in the night, but says God does not answer. The psalm does not treat this question as unbelief; it is spoken directly to "My God," which means the relationship is still being claimed even in distress.

questions.question: Who is speaking in this chapter?
questions.answer: The heading identifies the psalm as "A Psalm by David," but psalm headings can indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection. In the chapter itself, the speaker is an afflicted person who prays, suffers mockery, asks for rescue, and then leads praise in the assembly.

questions.question: What does "The Doe of the Morning" mean?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in the heading as something the psalm is "set to." Psalms preserves musical directions, but the ancient melodies and exact force of several performance terms are lost, so it is best read as an ancient performance or tune marker whose exact use is uncertain.

questions.question: Why does the speaker remember "Our fathers" in the middle of his complaint?
questions.answer: Verses 3-5 contrast the speaker's present anguish with Israel's remembered past. Earlier generations trusted, cried out, and were delivered; that memory sharpens the pain of the speaker's unanswered cry while also giving him language for continued appeal.

questions.question: Are the bulls, lions, and dogs literal animals?
questions.answer: The animal imagery makes the speaker's enemies feel powerful and predatory. Verse 16 places dogs alongside a company of evildoers, linking the animal language with human danger. The poem does not identify particular attackers or give enough detail to reconstruct a specific historical incident.

questions.question: What is happening in the lines about garments and clothing?
questions.answer: Verse 18 says the speaker's enemies divide his garments and cast lots for his clothing. Within the psalm, this is part of the humiliation and helplessness described in verses 16-18. Later Christian readers connect this verse with Jesus' crucifixion narratives, but the chapter itself presents it first as the suffering speaker's lament.

questions.question: Does the psalm actually turn from suffering to rescue?
questions.answer: Yes. The appeal in verses 19-21 still asks for deliverance, but verse 21 also says, "Yes, you have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen." After that, the speaker moves into public praise and tells the assembly that God heard the afflicted one.

questions.question: Who are "the humble" in verse 26?
questions.answer: The verse says the humble will eat, be satisfied, and praise Yahweh. In this chapter, they belong with those who seek Yahweh and with the afflicted person whom God has not despised. The psalm does not define the group more narrowly than that.

questions.question: Why does the ending speak about all nations and future generations?
questions.answer: The rescue leads to praise that expands beyond the speaker and even beyond Israel's immediate assembly. The psalm says the ends of the earth and the relatives of the nations will worship, because the kingdom is Yahweh's, and it ends with future generations being told what God has done.

glossary.def: A figure named in the heading, likely connected with the psalm's performance or collection, though the exact ancient role is not explained in the chapter.
The divine name used in this psalm. Yahweh is the God whom the speaker asks to rescue him and later praises as ruler over the nations.
A place name used in the phrase "Strong bulls of Bashan," part of the psalm's image of powerful threats surrounding the speaker.
The gathered group before whom the speaker promises to praise God after rescue.
